[0] everyday_reading (E): Folk meaning: in English 'otherwise' can be heard as 'and then also', and 'if ... else ...' as two separate rules that are each checked. In Java the condition is tested once and exactly one of the two branches runs.
[1] misconception (M) -> ConditionalIsSequence: wrong rule: if-else is the same as two separate ifs. Right rule: In if-else, c is tested once and exactly one of A or B runs, even if A changes the variables that c uses.
[2] misconception (M) -> ElseAlwaysExecutes: wrong rule: The else branch of an if-else statement always executes. Right rule: The else branch runs only when the if condition is false.
[3] misconception (M) -> BothBranchesExecute: wrong rule: Both the then branch and the else branch run. Right rule: Exactly one of the two branches runs.
[4] misconception (M) -> DuplicateCodeInBranches: wrong rule: Writes the same statements in both branches of an if-else. Right rule: Code common to both branches belongs before or after the if-else.
[5] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ConditionalIsSequence: Applies the if-else rule (LT) unevenly: on some traces runs both branches, re-tests the condition after the then branch to decide whether to run the else branch, or runs the else branch whatever the condition. (here mixing in: "if-else is the same as two separate ifs")
[6] misconception (M) -> BranchChosenByIntent: wrong rule: Which branch runs is decided by what the programmer meant or by code outside the if, not by whether the condition is true. Right rule: The then branch runs exactly when the condition evaluates to true at the moment it is tested; otherwise the else branch (if any) runs.

[0] names_the_element (N): The if-else statement is a two-way conditional: it executes one of two statements (or blocks) depending on a boolean condition.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Syntax: if (<boolean expression>) <statements T> else <statements F>; it executes one or the other, but not both: T if the condition is true, F otherwise.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Evaluate the condition once; if true execute the then branch, otherwise execute the else branch; then continue with the statement after the whole if-else (the condition is not re-tested).
[1] output_prediction (OP): Exactly one branch's effects occur; e.g. if (x > y) max = x; else max = y; leaves max equal to the larger value, and the coin flip prints either Heads or Tails, never both.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One execution reads the condition's variables and applies the effects of exactly one branch; a change made by the then branch to the condition's variables cannot cause the else branch to run.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): if-else is an if with a second branch for the false case; dropping the else gives a plain if in which the false case does nothing.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Either branch may itself be an if or if-else, which nests conditionals; without braces an inner else pairs with the innermost if.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): c ? a : b is the expression form of if (c) v = a; else v = b;: it yields a value of one branch, evaluating only the selected operand.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): An else-if chain is an if-else whose else part is another if-else, repeated; the final else catches all remaining cases.
[4] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Plan: two-way choice / alternative action - compute one of two results (max of two values, heads or tails, error message or quotient).

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ConditionalIsSequence: Swapping the two branches and negating the condition preserves behaviour; swapping the branches alone inverts it. Replacing if-else with two separate ifs is not equivalent when the then branch changes a variable used in the condition.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: else takes no condition: it is the branch for the false case of the preceding if; a further test needs else if (...). Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: Writing else (x > 0) stmt; the compiler reads (x > 0) as the start of an expression statement, which is not a valid statement, and reports an error.
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use if-else when exactly one of two actions must happen; use a plain if when nothing happens in the false case, an else-if chain or switch for more than two mutually exclusive cases, and c ? a : b when you only need to choose a value.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Code common to both branches belongs before or after the if-else. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: A statement duplicated in both branches and later edited in only one: the two cases silently diverge.
[4] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: An else must directly follow the then statement of an if. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: if (c) x = 1; y = 2; else x = 0;: the else has no matching if ('else without if').

An else-if chain is an if-else whose else part is another if.
Nesting puts an if or if-else inside a branch of another if-else; an else-if chain is the common case where the else branch is itself an if.
if-else extends if with a second block that runs exactly when the condition is false.
